l: Yi Yin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Yi Yin first lived as a farmer and delighted in the principles of Yao and Shun. He entered Tang’s service to instruct the people, urged Tang to attack Xia, and later placed Tai Jia in Tong until he repented and reformed.

l: the sovereign, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: The sovereign can present a man to Heaven but cannot make Heaven give that man the throne. The sovereign also cannot simply give the throne to another, because Heaven and the people determine acceptance.

l: Son of Heaven, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: The Son of Heaven appointed an officer to administer Xiang’s state and pay its revenues to him. This prevented Xiang from oppressing the people while allowing him to retain honour and wealth.

l: the people of the kingdom, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: The people accepted Shun after his administration caused them to rest securely. After the deaths of Yao and Shun, they followed Shun and Yu rather than the sons of the preceding sovereigns, while after Yu’s death they followed Qi rather than Yi.

l: the princes of the kingdom, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: The princes followed Shun after Yao’s death and Yu after Shun’s death. After Yu’s death, they went to Qi rather than Yi, recognizing Qi as the son of their sovereign.

l: You Bei, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: You Bei was made Xiang’s princedom. Its government and revenues were administered by an officer so that Xiang could not oppress its people.

l: Xia, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Xia was ruled by Jie, whose conduct made natural succession subject to displacement by Heaven. Tang attacked Xia in order to save its people.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: The Book of Poetry is cited concerning informing parents before marriage, the sovereign’s domain and service, filial thoughts, and the people of Zhou. Mencius warns that its individual terms and sentences must not be interpreted against the general scope.

l: Shun's marriage, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Shun’s marriage took place without informing his parents because doing so would have prevented him from marrying. Mencius says that marriage is the greatest of human relations.

l: Shun's accession to the throne, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Shun’s accession came from Heaven and the people rather than from Yao’s personal power to give away the throne. After Yao’s death, the people, princes, litigants, and singers turned to Shun instead of Yao’s son.

l: Yao's presentation of Shun to Heaven, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Yao presented Shun to Heaven by causing him to preside over sacrifices, which pleased all the spirits. Yao presented him to the people by causing him to administer affairs successfully, so that the people accepted him.

l: Yu's transmission of the throne to Qi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: After Yu’s death, Yi withdrew from the son of Yu, but the princes, litigants, and singers followed Qi. Mencius says this succession was determined by Heaven and by Qi’s relation to Yu, together with their differing service and virtue.

l: Yi Yin's service to Tang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Yi Yin entered Tang’s service because he believed that those who first apprehend principles should instruct those who are slower to understand them. He took upon himself responsibility for the kingdom and pressed Tang to attack Xia and save the people.

l: Tang's attack on Xia, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Tang’s attack on Xia was presented as an effort to destroy Jie’s rule and save the people. Yi Yin urged Tang to undertake this action according to the principles of Yao and Shun.

l: filial piety, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Filial piety is shown by Shun’s lifelong desire for the accord of his parents. Its highest achievement is honouring and nourishing one’s parents with the whole kingdom.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Benevolence does not store up anger or resentment against a brother. It regards him with affection and love and seeks to make him honourable and rich, as Shun did for Xiang.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Righteousness requires adherence to the principles prescribed by Yao and Shun. Yi Yin would not accept office or gifts contrary to righteousness, and his different course from other sages was judged by the shared aim of keeping his person pure.

l: Heaven's mandate, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Heaven’s mandate is shown through conduct and events rather than spoken instructions. It gives the throne when Heaven and the people accept a person, and it can displace a ruler like Jie or Zhou.

l: succession to the throne, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Succession may occur through Heaven’s choice of a worthy person or through natural succession to a sovereign’s son. Mencius says that both forms can embody the same principle of righteousness, depending on the virtue, service, and acceptance involved.

l: the principles of Yao and Shun, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: The principles of Yao and Shun are the teachings Yi Yin delighted in and used to instruct Tang and the people. They required benevolent government, righteousness, and benefits for the people.

l: Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Wan Zhang asks Mencius about stories concerning Confucius and Bai Li Xi. Mencius says Confucius lodged with Yan Chou You in Wei and with the city-master Chang after leaving Lu and Wei, not with the ulcer-doctor or the attendant Qi Huan. Mencius says Bai Li Xi was from Yu, did not remonstrate when Jin borrowed passage through Yu to attack Guo, later went to Qin, and became minister to the duke Mu of Qin. Mencius argues that Bai Li Xi was wise and possessed talents and virtue, and denies that he sold himself by feeding oxen.

l: Wan Zhang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Wan Zhang asks Mencius whether Confucius lodged with the ulcer-doctor in Wei and with the attendant Qi Huan in Qi. He also asks whether Bai Li Xi sold himself to a cattle-keeper of Jin for five rams' skins in order to gain an introduction to the duke Mu of Qin.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Mencius rejects the stories about Confucius lodging with the ulcer-doctor or Qi Huan and about Bai Li Xi selling himself to feed oxen. He explains where Confucius lodged, describes Bai Li Xi's actions concerning Yu, Jin, and Qin, and argues that Bai Li Xi was wise and had talents and virtue.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Confucius lodged with Yan Chou You in Wei and later with the city-master Chang after leaving Lu and Wei. He entered office according to propriety and retired from it according to righteousness, regarding obtaining office or not obtaining it as ordered by Heaven.

l: Wei, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Wei was a state in which Confucius lived with Yan Chou You. Confucius was dissatisfied in Wei and left it.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Righteousness is presented as the principle according to which Confucius retired from office. Lodging with the attendant Qi Huan would not have been according to righteousness.

l: Bai Li Xi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Bai Li Xi was a man of Yu who did not remonstrate when Jin sought passage through Yu to attack Guo. He later went to Qin, became minister to the duke Mu of Qin, and made his prince distinguished throughout the kingdom; Mencius denies that he sold himself to feed oxen.

l: Jin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Jin used a round piece of jade from Chui Ji and four horses of the Qu breed to borrow a passage through Yu to attack Guo.

l: the story of Bai Li Xi selling himself, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: The story says that Bai Li Xi sold himself to a cattle-keeper of Jin for the skins of five rams and fed oxen to find an introduction to the duke Mu of Qin. Mencius calls the story an invention by men fond of strange things.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Yu was the state of Bai Li Xi. When Jin sought passage through Yu to attack Guo, Gong Zhi Qi remonstrated against granting the request, while Bai Li Xi did not remonstrate; Bai Li Xi later left Yu after recognizing that its duke could not be remonstrated with.

l: the duke Mu of Qin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: The duke Mu of Qin was a ruler whom Bai Li Xi judged to be one with whom he would have a field for action. Bai Li Xi became his minister and made him distinguished throughout the kingdom and worthy of being handed down to future ages.

l: Qin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Qin was the state to which Bai Li Xi went after leaving Yu. In Qin, Bai Li Xi became minister to the duke Mu.

l: talents and virtue, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 8 .. Chapter 9
s: Talents and virtue are attributed to Bai Li Xi because he became chief minister of Qin and made his prince distinguished throughout the kingdom and worthy of being remembered by future ages.

l: Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Mencius discusses the conduct of Bo Yi, Yi Yin, Hui of Liu Xia, and Confucius, presenting them as contrasting sages whose examples influence others. He explains Zhou arrangements of ranks, territories, emoluments, friendship, presents, propriety, and the conditions under which Confucius accepted office. The unit also examines how rulers, common people, poverty, office, marriage, righteousness, and robbery relate to proper conduct.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Mencius describes the conduct and distinguishing qualities of Bo Yi, Yi Yin, Hui of Liu Xia, and Confucius. He explains principles governing rank, friendship, gifts, office, poverty, and propriety.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Bo Yi avoided bad sights and sounds, refused to serve disapproved princes or command people he did not esteem, and withdrew during confusion. His character is said to make the corrupt pure and the weak determined.

l: Yi Yin, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Yi Yin believed he could serve any ruler and command any people if service or command made them his sovereign or people. He took office in both good government and confusion and felt responsible for instructing the uninformed and securing benefits for all people.

l: Hui of Liu Xia, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Hui of Liu Xia served impure princes and accepted low office without shame. He did not conceal his virtue, murmur when dismissed, grieve in poverty, or reject village people, and his character is said to make the mean generous and the niggardly liberal.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Confucius left Qi by taking his rinsed rice and left Lu after saying he would depart shortly. He took office when proper, useful, or supported, tested whether his doctrines could be practiced, and left when they were not.

l: Zhou, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Zhou established five degrees of rank and six degrees of dignity, with assigned territories and emoluments. Zhou also received from Yin a rule concerning the punishment of robbers.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Heaven is described as producing people so that those informed earlier instruct those informed later. Heaven's places, offices, and emoluments are mentioned in relation to rulers honoring virtue and talents.

l: princes, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: The princes disliked the Zhou arrangement because they considered it injurious to themselves and destroyed its records. They are also said to take from their people as a robber does, though their gifts may be received when presented with propriety.

l: common people, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Common people employed in government offices received emoluments related to what they could earn by tilling fields. Their agricultural support varied according to the class and productivity of husbandmen.

l: sages, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: The sages are represented by Bo Yi as the pure one, Yi Yin as inclined to office, Hui of Liu Xia as accommodating, and Confucius as timeous. Confucius is described as combining these qualities in a complete concert.

l: friendship with virtuous scholars, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Friendship should be maintained without presumption based on age, station, or relatives. It is friendship with a person's virtue and does not admit assumptions of superiority.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Virtue is the proper basis of friendship and is honored by rulers and scholars. Hui of Liu Xia carried out his principles without concealing his virtue.

l: principles, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Principles should be carried into practice by those who hold office. Confucius accepted office when there was a likelihood that his principles would be practiced and left when they were not.

l: poverty, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Office is not normally sought because of poverty, though poverty can sometimes lead one to seek it. A person who takes office for that reason should choose low status and poverty rather than honor and riches.

l: office, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Office is appropriate when government is good, when principles may be practiced, when reception is proper, or when the state provides support. Holding office while one's principles are ignored is described as shameful for a scholar.

l: presents of friendship, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Presents of friendship express respect. They should be received when offered on a reasonable ground and according to propriety, but a gift obtained through robbery should not be accepted.

l: respect, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Respect is the feeling expressed in presents of friendship. Inferiors show respect to superiors through observance due to rank, while superiors show honor to inferiors by recognizing talents and virtue.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Propriety governs the offering and receiving of gifts and the conduct of rulers and scholars. A gift offered according to propriety may be received unless it was obtained through robbery.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Righteousness is used to judge whether gifts and offices are properly obtained or held. The text distinguishes refined judgments of righteousness from calling everyone who takes what is not theirs a robber.

l: robbery, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Robbery makes a gift improper even when the donor presents it with a reasonable explanation and proper manner. A robber who kills and takes property is described as deserving death without warning.

l: marriage, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 5
s: Marriage is not entered into solely to gain attendance from a wife, though there are times when one marries for that reason.

l: Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Wan Zhang and Mencius discuss when scholars may accept support from princes, why scholars without office should not receive princely pay, and how rulers should properly honor virtue and talents. They also discuss why scholars should not seek interviews with princes and how summons must follow propriety. Mencius explains that scholars make friends with virtuous scholars and, through study, with the men of antiquity. King Xuan of Qi asks about high ministers, learning that relatives should remonstrate and may dethrone a prince, while ministers of a different surname should leave the State if remonstrance fails.

l: Wan Zhang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Wan Zhang asks Mencius about scholars accepting support from princes, refusing princely pay, avoiding interviews with princes, and the proper forms for summoning different people.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Mencius explains the rules governing scholars, princely support, summons, friendship, and high ministers. He tells King Xuan of Qi that related high ministers should remonstrate repeatedly and may dethrone a prince, while ministers of a different surname should leave the State if the prince does not listen.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Confucius is cited as approving a forester who refused to go to the duke of Qi when summoned by an inappropriate flag. Mencius also explains that Confucius went immediately when summoned on the business of his office.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: King Xuan of Qi asks Mencius about the office of high ministers. He is initially moved and changes countenance when told that related high ministers may dethrone a prince, but then composes himself and asks about ministers of a different surname.

l: scholars, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Scholars may accept a prince's gifts to assist their necessities but should not accept princely pay without a regular office. Scholars without office should not presume to interview princes, and those of distinguished virtue make friends with virtuous scholars and study the men of antiquity.

l: princes, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Princes ought to assist people in their necessities and properly honor scholars of virtue and talents. They must use appropriate forms when summoning people and should listen to repeated remonstrance from high ministers.

l: high ministers, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: High ministers who are noble and relatives of the prince should remonstrate with him over great faults and may dethrone him if he repeatedly refuses to listen. High ministers of a different surname should remonstrate and then leave the State if their advice is rejected.

l: State, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: A prince who loses his State may properly accept a stated support from another prince. A high minister of a different surname should leave the State when repeated remonstrance fails.

l: the kingdom, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: A scholar whose virtue is most distinguished throughout the kingdom makes friends with all the virtuous scholars of the kingdom. If this is insufficient, the scholar studies and considers the men of antiquity.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Propriety governs whether scholars may accept princely support, receive princely pay, interview princes, and respond to summonses. It requires common men without office to avoid interviews with princes and requires appropriate summoning articles.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Righteousness is described as the way, with propriety as its door. A scholar accepts a prince's gift because the prince ought to assist people in their necessities, but refuses princely pay without a regular office.

l: talents and virtue, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: A prince who is pleased with virtue and talents should promote or support their possessor in the proper way. A person with extensive information may be a teacher, while a person with virtue and talents should not be summoned in an inappropriate manner.

l: office, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: People with regular offices may receive support from the prince, including keepers of the gates and watchmen. Confucius was in office when he went immediately after being summoned on the business of his office.

l: support from a prince, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: A scholar may accept a prince's gift of grain or other assistance for necessities but should not accept regular princely pay without an office. Proper support is offered initially with the prince's commission and then continued through the storekeeper and master of the kitchen without repeated direct commissions.

l: remonstrance, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: High ministers should remonstrate with a prince who has faults. Related ministers should do so repeatedly before dethronement becomes proper, while ministers of a different surname should leave the State after repeated unsuccessful remonstrance.

l: dethronement, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Dethronement is presented as the duty of noble high ministers who are relatives of the prince when the prince has great faults and refuses repeated remonstrance.

l: friendship with virtuous scholars, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: A scholar distinguished by virtue in a village, State, or kingdom makes friends with the virtuous scholars of that place. A scholar who remains unsatisfied ascends further by studying the poems, books, and histories of the men of antiquity.

l: interview with a prince, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Chapter 6 .. Chapter 9
s: Common men and scholars without office should not presume to interview a prince without following the proper forms. Even a man of virtue and talents may refuse when the prince summons him in a way that is inappropriate to his character.

l: Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: The unit concerns Mencius's debates with Gao and Gong Du about man's nature, arguing that it tends toward good and contains the beginnings of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. Mencius explains that circumstances, neglect, and failure to think can obscure this proper nature, while nourishment, reflection, and steadfast attention preserve it. He teaches that the human mind should seek its lost goodness, that learning consists in this recovery, and that people should cultivate what is great rather than what is small. The unit also distinguishes the nobility of Heaven from the nobility of man and states that righteousness may be valued above life and death avoided only at the cost of virtue.

l: Gao, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Gao compares man's nature to the qi-willow and to water, arguing that it is indifferent to good and evil and that benevolence is internal while righteousness is external. Mencius challenges these claims by arguing that fashioning virtue from man's nature does not require violence and that man's nature tends toward good.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Mencius argues that man's nature is constituted for good and that all people possess feelings corresponding to benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. He teaches that circumstances can obscure these qualities, while reflection, nourishment, and learning can preserve or recover them.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Confucius is cited as saying that what is held fast remains and what is released is lost, referring to the mind. He is also cited on the universal laws of human faculties and relations and on the principle of the nature expressed in an ode.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Heaven gives people their faculties and relations with specific laws and establishes the natural basis from which virtue may be cultivated. It also confers a nobler part of human constitution that should govern the inferior part.

l: man's nature, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Man's nature is presented as tending toward good and containing the beginnings of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. It can be weakened or obscured by harmful circumstances, neglect, and repeated exposure to evil, but proper nourishment allows it to grow.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Benevolence is identified as a principle arising from the feeling of commiseration and as part of man's proper nature. Mencius disputes the claim that it must be fashioned through violence and injury to man's nature.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Righteousness is identified as a principle arising from shame and dislike and as a path that people should follow. It is valued above life when the two cannot be preserved together, and it is included in the nobility of Heaven.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Propriety is identified as a principle arising from reverence and respect. It is one of the qualities with which people are furnished rather than something infused into them from outside.

l: knowledge, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Knowledge is identified as a principle arising from approving and disapproving. It is presented as an original human endowment that can be developed or neglected.

l: the human mind, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: The human mind contains proper goodness but can be stripped of it through repeated harmful influences, like the trees of Niu mountain. It is the object that learning must seek to recover, and through thinking it obtains the right view of things.

l: learning, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Learning has as its great end seeking the lost mind. It also requires giving the whole mind and bending the will to its subject rather than allowing attention to wander.

l: the nobility of Heaven, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: The nobility of Heaven consists of benevolence, righteousness, self-consecration, fidelity, and unwearied joy in these virtues. The men of antiquity cultivated it, while people of the present are criticized for pursuing the nobility of man and then abandoning it.

l: the nobility of man, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: The nobility of man consists of offices such as being a gong, a qing, or a da fu. It may come after the cultivation of the nobility of Heaven, but pursuing it while discarding the higher nobility is described as extreme delusion.

l: life, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Life is valued, but righteousness is valued more when the two cannot be preserved together. People therefore should not seek to preserve life through improper means.

l: death, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 16
s: Death is disliked, but there are things disliked more than death, so people may refuse actions that would avoid danger if those actions violate righteousness. The willingness to accept danger demonstrates that life is not the highest value.

l: Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Mencius discusses honour, benevolence, maturity, and instruction. He says men naturally desire honour, but true honour comes from benevolence and righteousness rather than from what men confer. He compares benevolence overcoming opposition to water overcoming fire, while warning that insufficient benevolence fails and encourages the non-benevolent. He also teaches that benevolence must mature and that students should follow the complete rules demonstrated by their teachers.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Mencius teaches that men should value benevolence and righteousness over honour, reputation, wealth, and fine clothing. He says benevolence must be brought to maturity and that instruction is properly followed when teachers and pupils apply the same complete rules.

l: men, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Men commonly desire to be honoured, but they possess something truly honourable within themselves without recognizing it. Men who are satiated with benevolence and righteousness do not desire the honours, wealth, or fine clothing that men confer.

l: honour, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Honour conferred by men is not good honour because one person can make another honourable and then make him mean again. True honour is associated with benevolence and righteousness.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Benevolence subdues its opposite as water subdues fire, but a small or incomplete amount may fail and encourage those who are not benevolent. Its value depends on being brought to maturity.

l: water, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Water is used as an example of something that subdues fire. A single cup of water cannot save a whole wagon-load of burning fuel.

l: fire, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Fire represents the force opposed to benevolence. A whole wagon-load of burning fuel cannot be extinguished by only one cup of water.

l: Yi, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 17 .. Chapter 20
s: Yi teaches men to shoot by drawing the bow to the full. His pupils follow the same rule.

l: Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Mencius teaches that rules of propriety remain important but must be understood in relation to circumstances, and that people can follow the ways of Yao and Shun through filial piety and fraternal duty. He argues that rulers and ministers should be guided by benevolence and righteousness rather than profit, conquest, excessive taxation, or enrichment. Mencius criticizes the five chiefs of the princes, the princes, and the Great officers for violating proper political order and praises those who love what is good. He advises the prince of Lu against employing an uninstructed army and rejoices that Yue Zheng loves what is good, since this is sufficient qualification for governing Lu.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Mencius explains that rules of propriety must be weighed according to the circumstances and rejects using profit as the basis of political counsel. He teaches that people can follow the ways of Yao and Shun through filial piety and fraternal duty, criticizes political wrongdoing, and praises love of what is good in a minister.

l: rules of propriety, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: The rules of propriety are said to be more important than eating or gratifying sexual appetite in ordinary comparisons. Mencius explains that their importance must be judged in relation to the importance of the competing matter and circumstance.

l: filial piety, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Filial piety and fraternal duty are described as the simple course followed by Yao and Shun. Confucius is cited as saying that Shun remained full of longing desire about his parents even at fifty.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Benevolence is presented as the proper basis for advising rulers and directing government. Mencius says a superior man serves his prince by leading him toward benevolence, and that a minister who loves what is good can help govern well.

l: profit, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Mencius rejects profit as the foundation for relations between rulers, ministers, fathers, sons, and brothers. He warns that serving a ruler by enriching him when the ruler lacks benevolence is to enrich a Jie.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Mencius says that counsel based on benevolence and righteousness could lead rulers to stop warfare and cause ministers and families to act according to those principles. He contrasts this with relations governed by profit and says a state guided by benevolence and righteousness can rise to royal sway.

l: five chiefs of the princes, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: The five chiefs of the princes are described as sinners against the three kings because they dragged princes to punish other princes. The most powerful chief, the duke Huan, established prohibitions concerning filial conduct, worthy officials, the old and young, offices, grain, embankments, and announcements to the sovereign.

l: princes, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: The princes were expected to attend the sovereign's court, cultivate their territories, honor the worthy, and appoint talented people. The princes of the present day are called sinners against the five chiefs because they violate the five prohibitions.

l: Great officers, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: The Great officers of the present day are called sinners against the princes because they anticipate and encourage their sovereigns' wickedness. Mencius distinguishes this from merely conniving at or aiding such wickedness, which he calls a smaller crime.

l: prince of Lu, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: The prince of Lu wanted to make Shen commander of his army and wanted to commit the administration of Lu to Yue Zheng. Mencius opposed employing an uninstructed people in war and was glad that Yue Zheng loved what is good.

l: Lu, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Lu is described as having five times 100 li square, more than the territory originally assigned to Zhou Gong. Mencius says a true royal ruler might diminish Lu rather than increase it and argues that its government should be directed toward benevolence.

l: taxation, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Bai Gui proposes taking only a twentieth of the produce as taxation. Mencius says that rate may suit Mo because it lacks many institutions and officials, but that the Middle Kingdom requires a fuller system and cannot reduce taxation below the arrangements of Yao and Shun without becoming a great Mo.

l: Yue Zheng, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Yue Zheng is described as lacking vigour, wisdom in council, and extensive information, but as loving what is good. Mencius says this quality is more than sufficient for governing Lu because it attracts good men and keeps calumniators, flatterers, and sycophants from dominating the government.

l: good, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 13
s: Love of what is good is presented as a decisive qualification for government. Mencius says that a minister who loves what is good attracts good thoughts from far away, while self-conceit drives good men away and allows calumniators, flatterers, and sycophants to appear.

l: Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 14 .. Chapter 16
s: Mencius explains the principles by which superior men accepted or left office, depending on a prince’s respect and willingness to act on their words. He describes how Heaven prepares people for great offices through suffering, toil, poverty, and frustration, citing Shun and others as examples. He teaches that distress can lead to reform and strength, while ease and pleasure can lead to a kingdom’s ruin. Mencius also says that refusing to teach someone can itself become a form of teaching.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 14 .. Chapter 16
s: Mencius explains when superior men should accept or leave office, emphasizing a prince’s respect and whether he acts on their words. He describes how hardship prepares people for great responsibilities and states that refusing to teach someone may itself teach him.

l: prince, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 14 .. Chapter 16
s: A prince may receive a superior man with great respect, but the man may leave if the prince does not act on his words or later becomes less polite. A prince who cannot follow a man’s doctrines may offer him only enough assistance to prevent death.

l: office, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 14 .. Chapter 16
s: Superior men accept office under different conditions involving a prince’s respect and willingness to practice their teachings. Heaven may confer a great office on someone after subjecting him to suffering, toil, hunger, poverty, and frustrated plans.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 14 .. Chapter 16
s: Shun is identified as a man who rose to prominence from among the channelled fields.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 14 .. Chapter 16
s: Heaven prepares a person for a great office by exercising his mind with suffering, burdening his body with toil and hunger, subjecting him to poverty, and confounding his undertakings. These hardships stimulate the mind, harden the nature, and supply incompetencies.

l: teaching, Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi), Chapter 14 .. Chapter 16
s: Teaching is described as having many forms. Refusing to teach a man may nevertheless teach him.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part I / Chapter 1
s: Mencius teaches that a person who exhausts their mental constitution comes to know their nature. By knowing their nature, they come to know Heaven. Preserving one's mental constitution and nourishing one's nature is the way to serve Heaven. A person establishes their Heaven-ordained being by cultivating personal character without being distracted by premature death or long life.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part I / Chapter 1
s: Mencius teaches that exhausting one's mental constitution leads a person to know their nature and then Heaven.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part I / Chapter 1
s: Heaven is known through knowing one's nature. Serving Heaven involves preserving one's mental constitution and nourishing one's nature.

l: mental constitution, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part I / Chapter 1
s: A person who exhausts their mental constitution knows their nature. Preserving it is part of the way to serve Heaven.

l: Heaven-conferred nature, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part I / Chapter 1
s: Knowing one's nature leads to knowing Heaven. Nourishing one's nature is part of the way to serve Heaven.

l: the way, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part I / Chapter 1
s: The way is to preserve one's mental constitution and nourish one's nature in order to serve Heaven. It also involves cultivating personal character while remaining undistracted by premature death or long life.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 2
s: Mencius teaches that everything has an appointment and that a man should submissively accept what may be correctly ascribed to it. He says that understanding Heaven's appointment means not standing beneath a precipitous wall. Death sustained while discharging one's duties may be ascribed to Heaven's appointment, but death under handcuffs and fetters may not.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says that there is an appointment for everything and that a man should submissively receive what may be correctly ascribed to it. He distinguishes between deaths that may and may not be ascribed to Heaven's appointment.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 2
s: Heaven has an appointment to which events may be correctly ascribed. Death sustained in the discharge of one's duties may be ascribed to Heaven's appointment, but death under handcuffs and fetters cannot.

l: the appointment of Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 2
s: An appointment exists for everything, and a man should submissively receive what may be correctly ascribed to it. The true idea of Heaven's appointment is connected with not standing beneath a precipitous wall.

l: death, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 2
s: Death sustained in the discharge of one's duties may correctly be ascribed to the appointment of Heaven. Death under handcuffs and fetters cannot correctly be so ascribed.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 3
s: Mencius distinguishes between two kinds of seeking and getting. When people gain through seeking and lose through neglect, seeking is useful for getting, and the things sought are within themselves. When seeking follows the proper course but getting depends on what is appointed, seeking does not cause getting, and the things sought are outside themselves.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 3
s: Mencius distinguishes between seeking that helps produce getting and seeking that does not.

l: seeking, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 3
s: Seeking is useful to getting when people gain through seeking and lose through neglect. Seeking is of no use to getting when it follows the proper course but getting is only as appointed.

l: getting, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 3
s: Getting is gained through seeking in one case, while in another case it occurs only as appointed and is not produced by seeking.

l: things sought for within ourselves, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 3
s: These are the things sought when seeking is useful to getting and people gain through seeking.

l: things sought outside ourselves, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 3
s: These are the things sought when seeking follows the proper course but getting is only as appointed.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 4
s: Mencius teaches that all things are already complete in us. He says the greatest delight comes from being conscious of sincerity through self-examination. He adds that vigorous effort at the law of reciprocity, when directed toward perfect virtue, brings one closest to its realization.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 4
s: Mencius teaches that all things are already complete in us. He says that self-examined sincerity is the greatest delight and that vigorous effort at the law of reciprocity brings one closest to perfect virtue.

l: all things, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 4
s: All things are said to be already complete in us.

l: sincerity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 4
s: Sincerity becomes a source of the greatest delight when one is conscious of it through self-examination.

l: law of reciprocity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 4
s: The law of reciprocity is to be practiced with vigorous effort. Such effort brings one closest to perfect virtue when seeking its realization.

l: perfect virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 4
s: Perfect virtue is something one seeks to realize. Vigorous effort at the law of reciprocity is described as the closest approximation to it.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 5
s: Mencius describes a way of living without understanding or examination. He says that pursuing the proper path throughout life without knowing its nature involves acting habitually without reflection. He identifies this as the way of multitudes.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 5
s: Mencius says that acting without understanding, doing so habitually without examination, and pursuing the proper path without knowing its nature is the way of multitudes.

l: multitudes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 5
s: The multitudes follow the proper path throughout life without understanding or examining what they do.

l: way of multitudes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 5
s: The way of multitudes consists of acting without understanding, acting habitually without examination, and pursuing the proper path without knowing its nature.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 6
s: Mencius says that a man may not be without shame. He teaches that recognizing and feeling ashamed of having lacked shame can prevent future occasions for shame. The unit concerns the relationship between a man, shame, and self-correction.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 6
s: Mencius says that a man may not be without shame. He teaches that feeling ashamed of having been without shame can prevent future occasions for shame.

l: man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 6
s: A man may not be without shame. If he becomes ashamed of having been without shame, he will afterwards not have occasion to be ashamed.

l: shame, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 6
s: Shame may be absent from a man, but recognizing and feeling ashamed of that absence can prevent future occasions for shame.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 7
s: Mencius says that the sense of shame is very important to a man. He observes that people who devise artful contrivances and versatile schemes do not let their sense of shame act. He asks what a person without this sense of shame has in common with other men.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 7
s: Mencius teaches that the sense of shame is of great importance and questions what a person without it shares with other men.

l: sense of shame, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 7
s: The sense of shame is described as very important to a man, but people skilled in artful contrivances and versatile schemes do not allow it to come into action.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 8
s: Mencius says that the able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity loved virtue and forgot their power. He asks whether the able and virtuous scholars of antiquity should be treated as an exception, and says they delighted in their own principles and were oblivious of the power of princes. Kings and dukes could not visit such scholars frequently unless they showed the utmost respect and observed all forms of ceremony, and therefore could not easily employ them as ministers.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 8
s: Mencius says that the able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity loved virtue and forgot their power. He also says that the able and virtuous scholars of antiquity delighted in their own principles and were oblivious of the power of princes.

l: able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 8
s: The able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity loved virtue and forgot their power.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 8
s: Virtue was loved by the able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity.

l: power, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 8
s: The able and virtuous monarchs of antiquity forgot their power. The power of princes was disregarded by the able and virtuous scholars of antiquity.

l: able and virtuous scholars of antiquity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 8
s: The able and virtuous scholars of antiquity delighted in their own principles and were oblivious of the power of princes. They required kings and dukes to show the utmost respect and observe all forms of ceremony before permitting frequent visits.

l: kings and dukes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 8
s: Kings and dukes were not permitted to visit the able and virtuous scholars of antiquity frequently unless they showed the utmost respect and observed all forms of ceremony. If they could not pay frequent visits, they could even less employ the scholars as ministers.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: Mencius advises Song Gou Jian about how to remain perfectly satisfied while travelling to different courts. He says one should be satisfied whether a prince accepts or rejects one's counsels by honoring virtue and delighting in righteousness. Mencius explains that a scholar preserves righteousness in poverty and stays on the proper path in prosperity. He also describes how the men of antiquity benefited the people when successful and cultivated personal character when unsuccessful.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: Mencius advises Song Gou Jian about travelling to different courts and securing perfect satisfaction. He teaches that virtue, righteousness, and adherence to the proper path should guide a scholar in poverty or prosperity.

l: Song Gou Jian, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: Song Gou Jian asks Mencius what is required to secure perfect satisfaction. He is advised to honor virtue and delight in righteousness.

l: scholar, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: A scholar does not let go of righteousness when poor and does not leave the proper path when prosperous. In this way, the scholar holds possession of himself and does not disappoint the expectations of the people.

l: men of antiquity, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: When the men of antiquity realized their wishes, they conferred benefits on the people. When they did not realize their wishes, they cultivated their personal character and became illustrious in the world.

l: people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: The people receive benefits when the men of antiquity realize their wishes. Their expectations are not disappointed when a prosperous scholar does not leave the proper path.

l: perfect satisfaction, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: Perfect satisfaction comes from honoring virtue and delighting in righteousness. It is maintained whether a prince acknowledges and follows one's counsels or does not do so.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: Virtue is to be honored and delighted in as a means of securing perfect satisfaction. The men of antiquity cultivated their personal character when their wishes were not realized.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: Righteousness is not to be abandoned by a poor scholar. It is part of the conduct that allows a person to remain perfectly satisfied.

l: the path of duty, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: A prosperous scholar does not leave the proper path. By remaining on it, the scholar does not disappoint the expectations of the people.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 9
s: When the men of antiquity were advanced to dignity, they made the whole kingdom virtuous as well.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 10
s: Mencius says that the mass of men wait for a king Wen before receiving a rousing impulse. Scholars distinguished from the mass rouse themselves without a king Wan. The unit contrasts the dependence of the mass of men with the self-motivation of distinguished scholars.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 10
s: Mencius says that the mass of men wait for a king Wen before receiving a rousing impulse, while scholars distinguished from the mass rouse themselves without a king Wan.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 10
s: The mass of men wait for a king Wen, and then they receive a rousing impulse.

l: mass of men, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 10
s: The mass of men wait for a king Wen before they receive a rousing impulse.

l: scholars distinguished from the mass, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 10
s: Scholars distinguished from the mass rouse themselves without a king Wan.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 11
s: Mencius says that if a man is given the families of Han and Wei and does not become elated when he looks upon himself, he is far beyond the mass of men.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 11
s: Mencius says that a man who receives the families of Han and Wei yet does not become elated when looking upon himself is far beyond the mass of men.

l: man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 11
s: A man is given the families of Han and Wei. If he then looks upon himself without being elated, he is far beyond the mass of men.

l: families of Han and Wei, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 11
s: The families of Han and Wei are added to a man as a test of whether he becomes elated when he looks upon himself.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 12
s: Mencius says that the people should be employed in ways intended to secure their ease. He says that even if the people are toiled, they will not murmur when their labor is intended to secure their ease. He also says that the people should be put to death in ways intended to preserve their lives. Even when they die, they will not murmur at him who puts them to death.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 12
s: Mencius says that the people should be employed to secure their ease and put to death to preserve their lives. He says that the people will not murmur under either circumstance when those purposes are intended.

l: the peasantry, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 12
s: The people are employed in a way intended to secure their ease. Though they are toiled, they will not murmur. They are also put to death in a way intended to preserve their lives, and though they die, they will not murmur at him who puts them to death.

l: putting the people to death, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 12
s: Putting the people to death is described as a way intended to preserve their lives. The people will not murmur at him who puts them to death.

l: death of the people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 12
s: The death of the people occurs when they are put to death in a way intended to preserve their lives. Though they die, they will not murmur at him who puts them to death.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: Mencius contrasts the effects of a chief with those of a true sovereign on the people. Under a chief, the people appear brisk and cheerful, while under a true sovereign they show deep contentment and do not murmur even when he slays them. The superior man transforms society through a spiritual influence that spreads like Heaven and Earth, advancing people toward goodness without their knowing who causes it.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: Mencius contrasts the effects of a chief and a true sovereign on the people. He describes how the superior man transforms society through spiritual influence.

l: chief, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: The chief leads all the princes, under whom the people look brisk and cheerful.

l: people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: The people appear brisk and cheerful under a chief. Under a true sovereign, they are deeply content, do not murmur even when he slays them, and do not think of his merit when he benefits them. They progress toward goodness without knowing who makes them do so.

l: true sovereign, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: The true sovereign brings the people deep contentment. Even when he slays them, they do not murmur, and when he benefits them, they do not think of his merit.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: Wherever the superior man passes through, transformation follows, and wherever he abides, his influence is spiritual. His influence advances people toward goodness without their knowing who causes it.

l: influence, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: The influence of the superior man is spiritual in nature. It flows abroad above and beneath like the influence of Heaven and Earth.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: Heaven is used as a comparison for the broad, flowing influence of the superior man.

l: Earth, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 13
s: Earth is used as a comparison for the broad, flowing influence of the superior man.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 14
s: Mencius compares kindly words, reputation for kindness, good government, and good instructions. He says reputation for kindness affects men more deeply than kindly words. Good instructions are loved by the people and gain their hearts, while good government is feared and gains their wealth.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 14
s: Mencius compares the effects of kindly words, reputation for kindness, good government, and good instructions.

l: kindly words, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 14
s: Kindly words do not enter so deeply into men as a reputation for kindness.

l: reputation for kindness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 14
s: A reputation for kindness enters more deeply into men than kindly words.

l: good government, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 14
s: Good government does not lay hold of the people as much as good instructions. The people fear good government, and good government gets the people's wealth.

l: people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 14
s: The people fear good government but love good instructions. Good government gets their wealth, while good instructions get their hearts.

l: good instructions, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 14
s: Good instructions lay hold of the people more than good government. The people love good instructions, and good instructions get their hearts.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Mencius explains that intuitive ability is the ability people possess without learning, while intuitive knowledge is knowledge they possess without thought. He says children instinctively love their parents and, as they grow, love their elder brothers. Filial affection for parents is the working of benevolence, and respect for elders is the working of righteousness. These feelings belong to all under heaven.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Mencius defines intuitive ability and intuitive knowledge, and explains the natural love children have for their parents and elder brothers.

l: intuitive ability, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Intuitive ability is the ability possessed by men without having been acquired by learning.

l: intuitive knowledge, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Intuitive knowledge is the knowledge possessed by men without the exercise of thought.

l: children, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Children carried in the arms know to love their parents, and when they are grown a little, they know to love their elder brothers.

l: parents (children's parents), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Children naturally know to love their parents.

l: elder brothers (children's elder brothers), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: When children are grown a little, they naturally know to love their elder brothers.

l: filial affection, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Filial affection for parents is the working of benevolence.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Benevolence works through filial affection for parents.

l: respect for elders, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Respect for elders is the working of righteousness.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: Righteousness works through respect for elders.

l: all under heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 15
s: The feelings of filial affection for parents and respect for elders belong to all under heaven.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 16
s: Mencius describes Shun living in deep, remote mountains among trees, rocks, deer, swine, and rude inhabitants. In that setting, Shun appears only slightly different from the local people. When Shun hears a single good word or sees a single good action, he responds with irresistible enthusiasm, like a stream or river bursting its banks.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 16
s: Mencius describes Shun's life in the deep retired mountains and his powerful response to goodness.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 16
s: Shun lives among trees, rocks, deer, and swine, and appears only slightly different from the rude inhabitants of the remote hills. When he hears a single good word or sees a single good action, he responds like a stream or river bursting its banks.

l: good word, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 16
s: A single good word causes Shun to respond with an irresistible flood of enthusiasm.

l: good action, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 16
s: A single good action causes Shun to respond with an irresistible flood of enthusiasm.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 17
s: Mencius says that a man should refrain from doing anything his own sense of righteousness tells him not to do. He should also avoid desiring anything that his sense of righteousness tells him not to desire. Mencius teaches that acting according to these restraints is all the man has to do.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 17
s: Mencius says that a man should not do what his own sense of righteousness tells him not to do or desire what it tells him not to desire. He teaches that acting this way is all the man has to do.

l: man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 17
s: A man is told to refrain from actions and desires that his own sense of righteousness rejects. Acting according to this guidance is presented as all he has to do.

l: sense of righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 17
s: The sense of righteousness tells a man what not to do and what not to desire. Following its guidance is described as sufficient for the man.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 18
s: Mencius says that men with intelligent virtue and prudence in affairs are generally shaped by sickness and troubles. He identifies the friendless minister and the concubine's son as people who keep their hearts under a sense of peril and take deep precautions against calamity. Mencius says that this experience makes them distinguished for their intelligence.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 18
s: Mencius says that men with intelligent virtue and prudence in affairs generally experience sickness and troubles. He explains that caution under peril and against calamity makes them distinguished for their intelligence.

l: men (Mencius's statement), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 18
s: Men who possess intelligent virtue and prudence in affairs are generally found to have experienced sickness and troubles. Their precautions against calamity contribute to their intelligence.

l: sickness and troubles, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 18
s: Sickness and troubles are associated with men who become intelligent in virtue and prudent in affairs.

l: friendless minister, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 18
s: The friendless minister keeps his heart under a sense of peril and uses deep precautions against calamity. On this account, he becomes distinguished for his intelligence.

l: concubine's son, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 18

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 19
s: Mencius distinguishes several kinds of people according to how they serve rulers and society. Persons who serve the prince do so for his countenance and favour, while ministers who seek the tranquillity of the State take pleasure in securing it. The people of Heaven believe they could carry out their principles throughout the kingdom if they held office, and therefore proceed to do so. Great men rectify themselves, and others are thereby rectified.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 20
s: Mencius describes the three things in which the superior man delights. The first is having both parents alive and brothers free from trouble. The second is having no shame before Heaven or people. The third is finding, teaching, and nourishing the most talented individuals in the kingdom. Being ruler over the kingdom is not among these delights.

s: Mencius states that the superior man has three delights, and that ruling the kingdom is not one of them.

s: The three delights are family well-being, freedom from shame before Heaven and people, and teaching and nourishing the kingdom's most talented individuals. Ruling the kingdom is excluded from the three delights.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 21
s: Mencius explains what the superior man truly values. Although the superior man may desire broad territory, a numerous people, and the tranquillization of the kingdom, these are not his highest enjoyment. His nature is determinately apportioned by Heaven and is neither increased by broad action nor diminished by poverty and retirement. Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge are rooted in his heart and manifest outwardly in his countenance, back, and limbs.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 21
s: Mencius explains that the superior man's highest enjoyment does not come from territory, population, or political influence. He teaches that the superior man's nature is fixed by Heaven and consists in benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 21
s: The superior man may desire wide territory and a numerous people, and may delight in tranquillizing the people within the four seas. His highest enjoyment lies instead in the qualities rooted in his nature, which remain undiminished in poverty and retirement and manifest throughout his body.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 21
s: Heaven determinately apportions what belongs by nature to the superior man.

l: the superior man's nature, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 21
s: The superior man's nature cannot be increased by a larger sphere of action or diminished by poverty and retirement. It includes benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge, which are rooted in the heart and expressed outwardly.

s: Benevolence is one of the qualities belonging by nature to the superior man. It is rooted in his heart and manifests as a mild harmony in his countenance, a rich fullness in his back, and an ordered movement of his limbs.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 21
s: Righteousness is one of the qualities belonging by nature to the superior man. It is rooted in his heart and contributes to its outward manifestation throughout his body.
